Three things about EAVS surprise people: variable codes are not stable across
years, "jurisdiction" does not mean county, and the package ships a curated
subset of the survey rather than all of it. This vignette covers each, and how to
work with the parts that are not curated.


``` r
library(tidyeavs)
```

## Codes move, and reuse is the real hazard

EAVS is organized in sections A through F: registration, UOCAVA, mail ballots,
polling places and precincts, provisional ballots, and participation. Within a
section, items are numbered, and the numbering is revised between cycles.

Renumbering on its own would be a nuisance. What makes it dangerous is that
retired codes get reused for different items. The precinct count is the worst
case in the shipped set:


``` r
eavs_items("precincts_total")[, c("year", "code", "codebook_label")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>    year code  codebook_label            
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>                     
#> 1  2016 D1a   D1a. Total Precincts      
#> 2  2018 D3a   Number of Precincts: Total
#> 3  2020 D2a   D2a Total Precincts       
#> 4  2022 D1a   D1a Total Precints        
#> 5  2024 D1a   D1a Total Precincts
```

The code is `D1a` in 2016, wanders to `D3a` and then `D2a`, and returns to `D1a`
in 2022. Checking only the first and last cycle suggests a stable code. In
between, `D1a` means votes cast in 2018 and Election Day poll-place voters in
2020, so a series pulled by code would silently mix three different quantities.

The `note` column exists for exactly this:


``` r
cat(strwrap(eavs_items("precincts_total")$note[1], 78), sep = "\n")
#> D1a='Total Precincts'. TRAP: D1a-2018='Votes Cast: Total'; D1a-2020='Voted
#> Poll Place Election Day'.
```

Search by code when you have a codebook in front of you, or by concept when you
know what you want:


``` r
eavs_items("C9a")[, c("concept", "year", "code")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   concept        year code 
#>   <chr>         <int> <chr>
#> 1 mail_rejected  2022 C9a  
#> 2 mail_rejected  2024 C9a
```

## Confidence, and where to be careful

Every mapping carries a rating. Anything below `high` means the definition
shifted and the `note` explains how:


``` r
d <- eavs_dictionary
table(d$confidence)
#> 
#>   high    low medium 
#>    201      1      3
subset(d, confidence != "high", select = c("concept", "year", "code"))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   concept             year code 
#>   <chr>              <int> <chr>
#> 1 polling_places_ed   2016 <NA> 
#> 2 partic_by_mail      2016 F1d  
#> 3 reg_forms_received  2024 A3a  
#> 4 ballots_cured       2024 C7b
```

## Jurisdictions are not counties

The unit is whatever files the survey, which varies by state. Wisconsin reports
roughly 1,850 municipalities, New England reports towns, Alaska and the
territories file one row each, and Maine files an extra statewide row carrying
only its UOCAVA totals:


``` r
j <- subset(eavs_jurisdictions, year == 2024)
sort(table(j$type), decreasing = TRUE)
#> 
#> municipality       county    territory    statewide 
#>         3477         2977            5            2
```

Two consequences worth planning around. County rollups drop anything whose
published code embeds no county, and say so:


``` r
panel <- eavs_load(2024, quiet = TRUE)
cty <- eavs_aggregate(panel, by = "county", concepts = "partic_total")
#> ! Dropping 1867 rows with no county in the published code.
#> ℹ Wisconsin's non-geographic serials, Maine's statewide row, Alaska, and the
#>   territories have none.
nrow(cty)
#> [1] 3044
```

Wisconsin is excluded even though its county is printed in every jurisdiction
name, and `eavs_jurisdictions` parses it into `county_name`. The reason is that
the municipalities straddling county lines include the City of Milwaukee:


``` r
wi <- subset(eavs_jurisdictions, year == 2024 & state_abbr == "WI")
sum(is.na(wi$county_name))
#> [1] 58
grep("MILWAUKEE|APPLETON", wi$jurisdiction_name[is.na(wi$county_name)], value = TRUE)
#> [1] "CITY OF APPLETON - MULTIPLE COUNTIES"  "CITY OF MILWAUKEE - MULTIPLE COUNTIES"
```

A Wisconsin county rollup would therefore be missing the state's largest city,
which is worse than not offering one. Use `county_name` for filtering and joins;
do not build county totals from it without deciding what to do about those rows.

## Who counts as a state

State-level output includes the territories and the District of Columbia,
because they file real data. `entity_type` makes a 50-state analysis one filter:


``` r
agg <- eavs_aggregate(panel, concepts = "partic_total")
table(agg$entity_type)
#> 
#>  district     state territory 
#>         1        50         5
subset(agg, entity_type != "state", select = c("state_abbr", "entity_type", "value"))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   state_abbr entity_type   value
#>   <chr>      <chr>         <dbl>
#> 1 AS         territory     10215
#> 2 DC         district     328871
#> 3 GU         territory     30283
#> 4 MP         territory     12610
#> 5 PR         territory   1283628
#> 6 VI         territory     15952
```

Puerto Rico is absent in midterm years, which will look like missing data in a
panel unless you know to expect it.

## The other 500 columns

The dictionary covers around 40 concepts, not the roughly 540 columns each file
carries. That is a curation choice, not a restriction: everything else is still
available, and the decoding that makes EAVS usable applies to all of it.


``` r
raw <- eavs_read(2024, quiet = TRUE)
dim(raw)
#> [1] 6461  537
decoded <- eavs_recode_missing(raw)
sum(vapply(decoded, is.numeric, logical(1)))
#> [1] 421
```

`eavs_read()` returns the file exactly as published, every column as text, so
FIPS codes keep their leading zeros. `eavs_recode_missing()` then decodes
sentinels across every numeric item, whether or not it is in the crosswalk.
Mail rejection reasons are a good example of something researchers often want:


``` r
reasons <- c(C9b = "late", C9c = "missing voter signature",
             C9e = "non-matching signature")
sapply(names(reasons), function(cd) sum(decoded[[cd]], na.rm = TRUE))
#>    C9b    C9c    C9e 
#> 103441  53511 197979
```

`eavs_missing_status()` works on these too, and once a column is attached to a
harmonized panel, `eavs_aggregate()` and `eavs_rate()` treat it like any other
numeric column:


``` r
tidy <- eavs_harmonize(decoded, year = 2024)
tidy$rejected_late <- decoded$C9b[match(tidy$fips_code, raw$FIPSCode)]
head(eavs_rate(tidy, "rejected_late", "mail_rejected")[, c("state_abbr", "rate", "n_both")], 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   state_abbr   rate n_both
#>   <chr>       <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 AK          0.169      1
#> 2 AL         NA          0
#> 3 AR          0.209     62
```

What you do not get is the cross-year work. You have to find each year's code
yourself, and the traps above are live: mail rejection reasons are `C4b`–`C4l` in
2018 and 2020 but `C9b`–`C9l` from 2022, and `C4b` means a drop-box count in the
later years. The 2016 file is a bigger step, with different column naming
throughout:


``` r
c(cols_2016 = ncol(eavs_read(2016, quiet = TRUE)), cols_2024 = ncol(raw))
#> cols_2016 cols_2024 
#>       595       537
grep("^A2", names(eavs_read(2016, quiet = TRUE)), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "A2"          "A2c_Other"   "A2_Comments"
grep("^A2", names(raw), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "A2a"        "A2b"        "A2c"        "A2Comments"
```

Same-day registration is `A2a` from 2018 on, but in 2016 the item is `A4a`, and
`A4a` in later years means mail registration forms. If you are doing single-year
work on an uncurated item, the package already handles the hard part. If you are
building a cross-year series from one, verify each year's code against that
year's codebook, and consider whether the concept belongs in the crosswalk
instead.
